name: Cows Milk
notes:
Whole cow's milk (3.25% fat), nutrition from USDA.

The animal side: a dairy cow gives about 13,300 kg of milk over her life worldwide. That's FAOSTAT's ~2,700 kg a year × ~5 productive years. In the US it's 31,300 kg (~11,000 kg a year, but cows are replaced faster). To keep milking she must calve every year. Only one calf replaces her, so about 3.5 calves per cow die worldwide (2.1 in the US), most raised for veal or beef for ~1.5 years. Each of those deaths is counted. A cow's neuron count (9.3 billion) is an estimate from her 480 g brain, using counts from related hoofed animals. It was raised from an older 3 billion projection on 2026-10-01.

Emissions are built from parts: methane and nitrous oxide from FAO's GLEAM model, feed from the corn, soy, alfalfa and hay rows, plus Poore & Nemecek's post-farm stages. Two big errors were fixed on 2026-09-24. Methane had been about 5× too high, and grazing land about 7× too low. Grazing land counts only pasture; feed cropland comes through the feed rows, so nothing is counted twice. US values (Pelton 2025, Eshel 2014) are much lower than world ones, because US cows give 4× more milk each.
land_types_note: Pasture and feed crops in the US, Europe and NZ (grassland and long-cleared forest), with some Brazilian soy in feed.
sentient_harm_explanation: Each dairy cow is eventually killed (or, in some countries, dies) once her milk yield drops, and to keep producing milk she must give birth to a calf roughly every year. Only about one of her calves is kept to replace her; the others die young or are raised and killed for veal or beef. Per cow we count: her own death (about 5 years old in the US: ~2 years growing up plus ~3 years milking; longer worldwide), about 2.1 calves in the US or 3.5 worldwide at roughly 1.5 years old each, and a lifetime of about 31,000 kg of milk in the US or 13,000 kg worldwide (lower-yield cows in South Asia and Africa pull the world figure down).

source.title: Kazu et al. (2014) — Cellular scaling rules for the brain of Artiodactyla include a highly folded cortex with few neurons (Frontiers in Neuroanatomy)
source.note: CORRECTION 2026-10-01: was 3.00e+09 (an older projection, not a count). Cows Milk — neuron_count (ESTIMATE, no direct count for this species): adult cattle brain 480.5 g (Ballarin et al. 2016, n = 150) → 9.3 bn whole-brain neurons. Kazu et al. 2014 (source 439) measured whole-brain neurons by isotropic fractionator in 5 artiodactyls (pig 57.8 g brain / 2.22 bn, springbok 102.1 g / 3.06 bn, blesbok 155.1 g / 3.90 bn, kudu 308.5 g / 6.09 bn, giraffe 528 g / 11.21 bn); fitted power law N = e^18.559 × M^0.712 (reproduces springbok within 1%). Brain mass source id 451.

source.note: Dairy cow — typical live weight of adult Holstein dairy cow ~680 kg; consistent with USDA breed average for high-producing commercial dairy herds.

source.title: FAOSTAT — Crops and Livestock Products (QCL): Raw milk of cattle, 2023
source.note: Milk (world) — lifetime milk per cow: FAOSTAT 2023 world cattle milk yield 2,685 kg per milk animal per year × productive life 4.97 yr = 13,340 kg ≈ 13,300 kg. World productive life 4.97 yr = 1 / cow-weighted average annual replacement rate (20.1%), using GLEAM 1.0 Table 2.3 regional replacement rates (NA 35%, W. Europe 31%, S. Asia 21%, Sub-Saharan Africa 10%, etc.) weighted by FAOSTAT 2023 milk-animal counts per region (source 226). Derived; low-yield, long-lived cows in South Asia and Africa dominate the world average. In India cow slaughter is restricted in many states, so 'per death' there is partly death from old age/abandonment rather than slaughter.

source.title: USDA NASS — Milk Production (February 2025): 2024 annual production per cow
source.note: Milk (US) — lifetime milk per cow: USDA NASS 2024 average 24,178 lb (10,967 kg) milk per cow per year × productive life 2.86 yr (1 / 35% annual replacement rate for North American dairy herds, GLEAM 1.0 Table 2.3, source 225) = 31,330 kg ≈ 31,300 kg. Cross-check: FAOSTAT 2023 US yield 10,923 kg → 31,200 kg. USDA NAHMS Dairy 2014 reports ~34% of cows removed per year plus on-farm deaths, consistent with a ~35% replacement rate.

source.title: FAO GLEAM 1.0 Model Description — Table 2.3 Herd parameters for dairy cattle, regional averages
source.note: Calves that die per cow (world): GLEAM herd model — calves born per cow-year = fertility × (1 − adult death rate) + replacement rate; over her productive life one calf becomes her herd replacement and the rest die. Per cow = fertility × (1 − adult death) / replacement rate, cow-weighted across GLEAM regions with FAOSTAT 2023 milk-animal counts = 3.54 (NA 2.13, W. Europe 2.57, S. Asia 3.29, Sub-Saharan Africa 6.77). Includes calves that die young on-farm (GLEAM calf death rates 8–50%; ~30% of these offspring deaths worldwide) as well as surplus calves raised and slaughtered for veal/beef. Derived.

source.title: FAO GLEAM 1.0 Model Description — Table 2.3 Herd parameters for dairy cattle, regional averages
source.note: Calves that die per cow (US): GLEAM 1.0 North America herd parameters — fertility 77%, adult death rate 3%, replacement rate 35%. Calves born per cow over her life = (0.77 × 0.97 + 0.35) / 0.35 = 3.13; minus 1 kept as her replacement = 2.13. Includes the ~8% of calves GLEAM assumes die young on-farm (≈12% of these offspring deaths); the rest are surplus bull and heifer calves sold for veal or dairy-beef. Derived.

source.title: FAO GLEAM 1.0 Model Description — Table 2.3 Herd parameters for dairy cattle, regional averages
source.note: Years in captivity of those calves (world): GLEAM age at slaughter for surplus dairy calves = age at first calving × (slaughter weight − birth weight) / (adult weight − birth weight), per region (e.g. NA 1.6–1.7 yr, S. Asia 0.6–1.1 yr, Sub-Saharan Africa 3.3 yr); calves dying young assumed ~0.08 yr (~1 month, assumption). Weighted over all offspring deaths and FAOSTAT cow counts = 1.62 yr. GLEAM assumes surplus calves are mostly fattened for beef rather than killed as very young veal, so this is higher than a veal-only figure (~0.1–0.5 yr). Derived.

source.title: FAO GLEAM 1.0 Model Description — Table 2.3 Herd parameters for dairy cattle, regional averages
source.note: Years in captivity of those calves (US): GLEAM 1.0 North America — surplus dairy bull calves fattened to 605 kg (≈1.68 yr) and heifers to 564 kg (≈1.56 yr), from age at first calving 2.1 yr × (slaughter − birth weight)/(adult − birth weight); ~8% die young (~0.08 yr, assumed). Weighted = 1.46 yr. Consistent with most US dairy bull calves now going to dairy-beef / beef-on-dairy feedlots rather than veal (US veal is a small share). Derived.

source.title: FAO/BfR — Tables on Weight Yield of Food and Retention Factors
source.note: Milk — yield_fraction 1.0: Feed conversion ratios for dairy are already expressed per kg milk output; no further live-weight-to-edible conversion is needed. Milk is consumed as produced.

source.title: Poore & Nemecek (2018) — Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers (Science)
source.note: Milk — total GHG: 3.15 kg CO2e/kg (global mean — OWID labels the P&N series 'global average'; not a median — cradle-to-retail). Includes enteric fermentation CH4, manure N2O, feed crop production emissions, on-farm energy, processing, transport, and retail. System boundary: full supply chain (not farm-gate only). This is the authoritative P&N 2018 value for fluid cow milk. P&N stage split (OWID supply-chain chart, source 72): land-use change 0.51, farm 1.51, animal feed 0.24, processing 0.15, transport 0.09, retail 0.27, packaging 0.10, losses 0.27. CORRECTION 2026-09-24: note previously called 3.15 a 'global median'; OWID publishes it as the global average (mean).

source.title: Our World in Data — GHG Emissions per kg of Food (Poore & Nemecek 2018)
source.note: Milk — total GHG: 3.15 kg CO2e/kg confirmed from OWID grapher CSV download of the Poore & Nemecek 2018 dataset. The OWID chart directly publishes P&N 2018 data; the CSV value for milk is 3.15, corroborating the P&N source. Full supply-chain cradle-to-retail boundary. This is the global average (mean), not a median.

source.title: Pelton et al. (2025) — Spatially Resolved Greenhouse Gas Emissions of U.S. Milk Production in 2020 (Environ. Sci. Technol. 59:9552)
source.note: US: derived cradle-to-retail. Pelton et al. 2025 farm gate 1.38 kg CO2e/kg FPCM (milk-allocated, incl. feed LUC, AR6) + raw-milk transport, processing & packaging 0.16 (Pelton 2026, source 293) + retail losses ~0.21 and distribution/retail ~0.08 (Thoma 2013 12% retail loss, source 294) = ~1.8.

source.title: Thoma et al. (2013) — Greenhouse gas emissions from milk production and consumption in the United States: a cradle-to-grave LCA circa 2008 (Int. Dairy J. 31:S3)
source.note: US: Thoma et al. 2013 cradle-to-grave 2.05 kg CO2e per kg milk CONSUMED (circa 2008), which includes a 20% consumer loss; per kg purchased 2.05 x 0.8 = 1.64 (still includes consumer refrigeration and packaging disposal). Farm gate 1.23 kg CO2e/kg FPCM; 72% of emissions before the farm gate.

source.title: Poore & Nemecek (2018) — Data S2 (aaq0216_DataS2.xls), 'Results - Global Totals' sheet
source.note: CORRECTION 2026-09-24: replaced 0.0001 ha/kg (source 55) — it was ~1 m2 per kg milk, close to P&N's 10th-percentile farm (1.11 m2/kg) rather than a typical value (P&N milk mean 8.95, median 2.1 m2/kg), and its note said it included arable feed land, which the feed rows already count (double count). It also left out fresh grass grazing (~29% of the world dairy diet). This field is now GRAZING LAND ONLY (permanent pasture/meadow); feed-crop land comes from the feed rows. New value from Poore & Nemecek 2018 Data S2, sheet 'Results - Global Totals', row Milk: land use per kg (Food Balance Sheet unit, 2009-11) = arable 1.327 + fallow 0.402 + permanent pasture 6.275 m2/kg. Grazing = permanent pasture 6.275 m2/kg. Allocation: P&N uses economic allocation between milk and dairy-herd beef; from the same sheet, milk 6.275 x 470,267 kt = 295 Mha and dairy-herd beef 13.667 x 31,425 kt = 43 Mha, so milk carries ~87.3% of dairy-herd pasture. Rescaled to the GLEAM ~0.92 milk share used for the gas and feed fields (source 290): 6.275 x 0.92 / 0.873 = 6.61 m2/kg = 0.00066 ha/kg. Check: 6.6 grazing + ~2.35 feed-crop land (feed rows) = ~8.95 m2/kg, equal to P&N's resampled mean (8.95). Caveats: P&N say their pasture is biased LOW (no LCAs from much of Africa and Central Asia); 'permanent pasture' includes hay meadows, so it may partly overlap the grass-hay feed row (up to ~1 m2/kg).

source.title: Eshel et al. (2014) — Land, irrigation water, greenhouse gas, and reactive nitrogen burdens of meat, eggs, and dairy production in the United States (PNAS 111:11996), SI workbook
source.note: CORRECTION 2026-09-24: milk had no US grazing value (the US view fell back to the wrong world 0.0001). US value from Eshel et al. 2014 SI workbook (sheets 'PartitioningResources' and 'PartitioningPerCal'): US dairy uses 49.2 million acres of pasture/range per year (2000-2010 mean, ~20.0 Mha incl. the 100.5% domestic-disappearance adjustment; uncertainty +-57%), i.e. 6.9% of US grazing feed. US milk output over the same period (same workbook, USDA 2001-2010 mean) = 179,308 million lb = 81.3 Mt -> 2.46 m2 grazing land per kg milk. Eshel charge all dairy-herd feed to dairy products (the workbook computes an 8.3% culled-dairy share but does not use it), so Pelton 2025's 81% milk allocation (source 292, used for the US gas and feed fields) is applied: 2.46 x 0.81 = 1.99 m2/kg = 0.0002 ha/kg. Lower than world because most US milk comes from confined herds (GLEAM N. America ration: fresh grass 14.4% of DM). Eshel's pasture counts all US grassland pasture, range and grazed forest by feed share, similar to P&N's FAOSTAT-type area. 2000-2010 data; US milk output is ~26% higher now (2023), so today's value may be somewhat lower.

source.title: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (2012) — Water Footprint of Animal Products (Report 48, Vol. 1)
source.note: Dairy pasture — green water evapotranspiration: global production-weighted average ~6,500,000 L/ha/yr (650 mm/yr) for permanent pasture. Reflects mix of tropical high-ET systems (~800–1,200 mm/yr) and temperate lower-ET systems (~400–700 mm/yr).

source.title: Allen et al. (1998) — FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 56: Crop Evapotranspiration
source.note: Dairy pasture — ET corroboration: FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method yields global area-weighted ET of ~600–700 mm/yr for permanent pasture, consistent with the 650 mm/yr (6,500,000 L/ha/yr) value used for dairy.

source.title: Poore & Nemecek (2018) — Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers (Science)
source.note: Milk — native_fraction 0.8: approximately 80% of dairy land is on long-established agricultural land with minimal ongoing ecosystem conversion. Dairy farming is predominantly near infrastructure; less tropical deforestation pressure than beef.

source.title: FAO (2013) — Greenhouse gas emissions from ruminant supply chains: A global life cycle assessment (GLEAM; Opio et al.)
source.note: CORRECTION 2026-09-24: replaced 0.24 (attributed to Poore & Nemecek 2018) and 0.22 (attributed to FAO GLEAM v3) kg CH4/kg milk — neither source supports them: at GWP 28, 0.24 kg CH4 alone is 6.7 kg CO2e, twice P&N's entire 3.15 kg CO2e/kg milk cradle-to-retail total (0.24 may be FAO 2010's 2.4 kg CO2e/kg with a slipped decimal — unconfirmed). New value from FAO 2013 GLEAM ruminant report: global cow milk 2.8 kg CO2e/kg FPCM (cradle to farm gate, protein allocation between milk and dairy-herd meat, GWP CH4=25); CH4 = 50% of total (enteric 46.5%, manure ~3.8%). 0.50 x 2.8 / 25 = 0.056 kg CH4/kg FPCM (~ per kg raw milk; FPCM is standardised to 4.0% fat / 3.3% protein). Converted to gas mass with the source's own GWP100; the app re-weights with CH4=28, N2O=265.

source.title: FAO (2010) — Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Dairy Sector: A Life Cycle Assessment
source.note: CORRECTION 2026-09-24: replaces the 0.24/0.22 entries (see first entry). FAO 2010 dairy-sector LCA: 2.4 kg CO2e/kg FPCM global average (milk-allocated, GWP CH4=25), methane ~52% of total. 0.52 x 2.4 / 25 = 0.050 kg CH4/kg FPCM. Converted to gas mass with the source's own GWP100; the app re-weights with CH4=28, N2O=265.

source.title: Our World in Data — Food Greenhouse Gas Emissions Across the Supply Chain (Poore & Nemecek 2018)
source.note: CORRECTION 2026-09-24: replaces the 0.24/0.22 entries (see first entry). Consistency check against Poore & Nemecek's own stage split (OWID): milk 'Farm' stage = 1.51 kg CO2e/kg (enteric + manure + on-farm energy; P&N GWP CH4=34). Even if the whole farm stage were CH4 that is only 1.51/34 = 0.044 kg CH4/kg; assuming ~85% of it is CH4 (rest manure N2O and energy) gives ~0.038. Derived bound, hence confidence 2.

source.title: Pelton et al. (2025) — Spatially Resolved Greenhouse Gas Emissions of U.S. Milk Production in 2020 (Environ. Sci. Technol. 59:9552)
source.note: US: Pelton et al. 2025 (US milk 2020, 1.38 kg CO2e/kg FPCM farm gate, biophysical allocation 81% milk / 19% meat, AR6 GWP biogenic CH4=27). Enteric 27% of total = 0.373 kg CO2e -> 0.0138 kg CH4; manure 19% of total, of which 73% CH4 = 0.191 kg CO2e -> 0.0071 kg CH4. Sum 0.0209 kg CH4/kg FPCM (US raw milk ~3.95% fat, so FPCM ~ per kg milk). Converted to gas mass with the source's own GWP100; the app re-weights with CH4=28, N2O=265.

source.title: FAO (2013) — Greenhouse gas emissions from ruminant supply chains: A global life cycle assessment (GLEAM; Opio et al.)
source.note: CORRECTION 2026-09-24: replaced 0.004 (attributed to Poore & Nemecek 2018 and to FAO GLEAM v3) — about 3x too high, and its note said it included feed-crop fertiliser N2O, which the feed rows already count (double counting). New value from FAO 2013 GLEAM, manure N2O only: GLEAM's global dairy split (Figure 5) gives N2O ~29% of 2.8 kg CO2e/kg FPCM; excluding 'fertiliser & crop residues' N2O (counted in feed rows) leaves applied & deposited manure (~17%) + manure-storage N2O (~5%) ~ 18-22% -> 0.20 x 2.8 / 298 = 0.0019 kg N2O/kg FPCM. The pie-chart labels are hard to match exactly, hence confidence 2. Converted to gas mass with the source's own GWP100; the app re-weights with CH4=28, N2O=265.

source.title: Our World in Data — Food Greenhouse Gas Emissions Across the Supply Chain (Poore & Nemecek 2018)
source.note: CORRECTION 2026-09-24: replaces the 0.004 entries (see first entry). Consistency check against Poore & Nemecek's stage split (OWID): Farm stage 1.51 kg CO2e/kg minus CH4 (~0.038 x 34 = 1.29) minus on-farm energy (~0.05) leaves ~0.17 kg CO2e for manure N2O -> 0.17 / 298 = 0.0006 kg N2O/kg milk. Derived bound, confidence 2.

source.title: Pelton et al. (2025) — Spatially Resolved Greenhouse Gas Emissions of U.S. Milk Production in 2020 (Environ. Sci. Technol. 59:9552)
source.note: US: Pelton et al. 2025 — manure = 19% of 1.38 kg CO2e/kg FPCM, 27% of that N2O = 0.071 kg CO2e -> / 273 (AR6) = 0.00026 kg N2O/kg FPCM. Manure/pasture N2O only; feed-crop fertiliser N2O sits in Pelton's feed categories and in our feed rows. Converted to gas mass with the source's own GWP100; the app re-weights with CH4=28, N2O=265.

source.title: Our World in Data — Food Greenhouse Gas Emissions Across the Supply Chain (Poore & Nemecek 2018)
source.note: CORRECTION 2026-09-24: replaced 0.08 (attributed to Poore & Nemecek 2018) and 0.07 (attributed to GLEAM v3) — both covered only on-farm energy, so every stage after the farm gate was missing and milk was not comparable to other foods' cradle-to-retail totals. New value = on-farm energy ~0.05 kg CO2/kg (GLEAM 2013 Table E9 direct on-farm energy factors: 0.02-0.03 developing, 0.05-0.07 OECD; source 290) + Poore & Nemecek post-farm stages for milk (OWID): processing 0.154 + transport 0.093 + retail 0.265 + packaging 0.100 + supply-chain losses 0.274 = 0.886 kg CO2e/kg. 0.05 + 0.886 = 0.94. Post-farm stages are stored here as CO2e (they include small refrigerant and non-CO2 amounts). Excludes feed-crop production and land-use change (feed rows).

source.title: Pelton, Bernal & Kurt (2026) — Spatially Resolved Greenhouse Gas Emissions from U.S. Dairy Products (Environ. Sci. Technol. 60:17810)
source.note: US: on-farm energy 5% + feed milling/transport ~1.7% of 1.38 kg CO2e/kg FPCM (Pelton 2025, source 292) = 0.092; post-farm ~0.45 = raw-milk transport, processing and packaging 0.16 (Pelton 2026: farm = 88% of 1.34 kg CO2e/kg packaged fluid milk at the processing gate) + retail-stage losses ~0.21 (Thoma et al. 2013, source 294: 12% of milk lost at retail -> 1/0.88 x ~1.54) + distribution and retail refrigeration ~0.08 (estimate; P&N world transport 0.093 + retail 0.265 is higher, so this may be low). 0.092 + 0.45 = 0.54. Derived, confidence 2.

source.title: FAO (2013) — Greenhouse gas emissions from ruminant supply chains: A global life cycle assessment (GLEAM; Opio et al.)
source.note: CORRECTION 2026-09-24: replaced 0.92 kg/kg milk (Alberta Milk source 37 + Dairy Global source 39: one Alberta high-yield 'lifetime' ration of 1.67 kg feed/kg milk split 55/25/10/7%, applied worldwide, summing to 97%, no silage/pasture/residues, 100% charged to milk). World corn: grains 8.6% x 2.43 = 0.209 kg DM / 0.845 (15.5% moisture) = 0.247 kg as-fed (all grains counted as corn; Europe also feeds wheat/barley) + corn silage (assumed 40% of 'legumes & silage' = 0.131 kg DM x 0.70) = 0.092 -> 0.34 kg corn/kg milk. World intake: GLEAM 2013 milk-allocated enteric CH4 = 46.5% x 2.8 / 25 = 0.052 kg CH4/kg FPCM; IPCC 2019 Refinement Table 10.12 methane yield for low/medium-producing cows ~21.4 g CH4/kg DM -> 2.43 kg DM feed per kg milk. Ration from GLEAM 2013 Table B7 (dairy cattle ration by region), weighted by approximate 2023 regional cow-milk shares (FAOSTAT, rounded): fresh grass 29% and crop residues/leaves/tops 21% (pasture or free by-products -> no feed row), hay 16.6%, legumes & silage 13.5%, grains 8.6%, oilseed meals 5.9%, bran/distillers grains 2.4% (by-products -> omitted, small allocated burden). Corn silage has no feed entry, so it is represented as corn-grain equivalent by land (and hence roughly by emissions, since fertiliser per ha is similar): US 2023 corn grain 177.3 bu/ac = 11.1 t/ha as-fed vs corn silage 20.1 short tons/ac as harvested x 35% DM = 15.8 t DM/ha (USDA NASS Crop Production 2023 Summary, source 120) -> 1 kg silage DM ~ 0.70 kg corn grain. Allocation: the per-kg values use milk-allocated intake, consistent with the gas fields (world: GLEAM protein allocation ~0.90-0.96 to milk, Table B22; US: Pelton 81% milk / 19% dairy-herd meat) — derived by dividing the SOURCE'S milk-allocated enteric CH4 by the IPCC 2019 methane yield per kg DM, so the same allocation carries into feed.

name: Yogurt
notes:
Plain whole-milk yogurt, nutrition from USDA. Every per-kg impact is cow milk × 1.15 kg of milk per kg of yogurt: feed, methane, grazing land and lifetime output (about 11,600 kg of yogurt per cow worldwide, 27,200 in the US). It carries the same cow and calf deaths as milk.

CO2 adds yogurt-specific processing (FAO 2010, Europe) on top of milk's on-farm energy and post-farm stages. The US cross-check (Pelton 2026) gives 2.4–4.4 kg CO2e/kg, but that includes strained Greek yogurt, which uses about 3× more milk.

Availability (~68 Mt) is from a market report with no primary source (confidence 1). FAOSTAT's yogurt figure leaves out the US and most of Asia.
land_types_note: Pasture and feed crops in the US, Europe and NZ (grassland and long-cleared forest), with some Brazilian soy in feed.
sentient_harm_explanation: Yogurt is made from cow's milk (about 1.15 kg of milk per kg of yogurt), so it carries the same animal deaths as milk. Each dairy cow must give birth roughly every year to keep producing milk; only about one of her calves is kept to replace her, and the rest die young or are raised and killed for veal or beef. Per cow we count: her own death (about 5 years old in the US; longer worldwide), about 2.1 calves in the US or 3.5 worldwide at roughly 1.5 years old each, and a lifetime of about 27,000 kg of yogurt in the US or 11,600 kg worldwide.

name: Butter
notes:
Salted butter, nutrition from USDA. It takes about 22 kg of milk to make 1 kg of butter. The skim milk and buttermilk left over are sold as food too, so butter carries only its value share: about 8.2 kg of milk per kg. This uses Flysjö 2011's fat:protein value split, as in Danish dairy LCAs. Every per-kg impact (feed, methane, grazing land, lifetime output) is milk × 8.2.

CO2 is milk's on-farm energy × 8.2, plus butter's own processing, packaging and transport (1.6 kg CO2e/kg, from the Arla butter LCA). Milk's own retail stages are NOT multiplied; an earlier version did that and overstated butter (fixed 2026-09-24).

The build check warns that butter's gas-by-gas total doesn't match its published LCA totals (Arla 9.0, Poore & Nemecek-derived 20.1, US 14.3). This is a known open item: the published studies use different allocations.
land_types_note: Pasture and feed crops in the US, Europe and NZ (grassland and long-cleared forest), with some Brazilian soy in feed.
sentient_harm_explanation: Butter is made from cow's milk, so it carries the same animal deaths as milk. It takes about 22 kg of milk to make 1 kg of butter, but the skim milk and buttermilk left over are sold as food too, so butter is charged with only its value share, about 8 kg of milk per kg. Per cow we count: her own death (about 5 years old in the US; longer worldwide), about 2.1 calves in the US or 3.5 worldwide at roughly 1.5 years old each, and a lifetime share of about 3,800 kg of butter in the US or 1,600 kg worldwide.

name: Whey Protein
notes:
Whey protein concentrate powder (WPC80), nutrition averaged from three unflavoured USDA-branded products.

Whey is left over from cheesemaking. It takes over 100 kg of milk to make 1 kg of whey protein, but cheese is the main product. The cheese plant charges whey only 4.8% of the milk's burden (Bacenetti et al. 2019), so whey protein carries about 5 kg of milk per kg. Every per-kg impact (feed, methane, grazing land, lifetime output) is milk × 5.

CO2 adds whey-processing stages (ultrafiltration, spray drying, packaging, transport) from CarbonCloud's verified benchmark. The build check warns that the gas total doesn't match the published totals (CarbonCloud 7.3, Bacenetti 5.9); allocation choices drive that gap. Availability is US-only (USDA 2024) and used for every region; world output is likely 2–3× higher.

Vitamins and minerals come from a stand-in USDA record (generic whey-based protein powder) because the branded labels don't list them.
land_types_note: Pasture and feed crops in the US, Europe and NZ (grassland and long-cleared forest), with some Brazilian soy in feed.
sentient_harm_explanation: Whey protein is made from the whey left over when milk is turned into cheese, so it carries the same animal deaths as milk. It takes over 100 kg of milk to make 1 kg of whey protein powder, but cheese is the main product and gets most of the blame, so whey protein is charged with only its value share, about 5 kg of milk per kg. Each dairy cow must give birth roughly every year to keep producing milk; only about one of her calves is kept to replace her, and the rest die young or are raised and killed for veal or beef. Per cow we count: her own death, about 2.1 calves in the US or 3.5 worldwide at roughly 1.5 years old each, and a lifetime share of about 6,300 kg of whey protein in the US or 2,700 kg worldwide.

name: Cheddar
notes:
Cheddar from cow's milk, nutrition from USDA. USDA's milk-equivalent puts it at about 9.2 kg of milk per kg of cheese. The whey that's sold takes 4.8% of the burden, so cheddar carries 8.8 kg. Every per-kg impact (feed, methane, grazing land, lifetime output) is cow milk × 8.8, so it carries the same cow and calf deaths as milk.

CO2 is milk's on-farm energy × 8.8, plus Poore & Nemecek's cheese processing, transport, retail and packaging (1.38 kg CO2e/kg). Supply-chain losses are left out, since they'd scale the milk footprint already counted. Published totals for comparison: US cheddar 8.6 kg CO2e/kg (Kim 2013), and the all-cheese global average 23.9 (Poore & Nemecek).

Availability is US production only (1.7 Mt, USDA 2024), used for every region. FAOSTAT doesn't break cheese out by type.
land_types_note: Pasture and feed crops in the US, Europe and NZ (grassland and long-cleared forest), with some Brazilian soy in feed.
sentient_harm_explanation: Cheddar is made from cow's milk, so it carries the same animal deaths as milk. It takes about 9 kg of milk to make 1 kg of cheddar; the leftover whey is sold too, so cheddar is charged a little less, about 8.8 kg of milk per kg. Each dairy cow must give birth roughly every year to keep producing milk; only about one of her calves is kept to replace her, and the rest die young or are raised and killed for veal or beef. Per cow we count: her own death, about 2.1 calves in the US or 3.5 worldwide at roughly 1.5 years old each, and a lifetime share of about 3,560 kg of cheddar in the US or 1,510 kg worldwide.

name: Goat Milk
notes:
Goat's milk, nutrition from USDA. Unlike cow milk, this reflects the world-average milking goat, mostly small multi-purpose animals in South Asia and Africa. That goat gives only ~95 kg of milk a year (FAOSTAT), versus ~2,700 kg for a cow. That low yield drives everything below. A commercial European or US dairy goat gives 600–1,000 kg a year and would score much better.

Emissions come from FAO's GLEAM model: 5.2 kg CO2e per kg, split into methane, manure nitrous oxide and energy. Feed intake (~6.5 kg dry matter per kg milk) is back-calculated from GLEAM's methane with the IPCC 2019 rule for goats. It's split using GLEAM's goat milk ration: grass, hay, crop residues, a little oilseed meal and grain. Grazed grass becomes pasture area (Mottet 2017: ~1,380 kg grass grazed per ha per year). Crop residues have no crop footprint.

Animal deaths: each doe gives ~510 kg of milk in her life, and about 4.2 kids per doe die (raised for meat, ~1.3 years). No goat brain has been counted. The 3.6 billion neurons are estimated from goat brain size using counts from related hoofed animals.
land_types_note: Mostly grazing and crop stubble in semi-arid India, Pakistan, Sudan and the Sahel; plus Mediterranean and western European dairy goats (France, Spain, Netherlands, Greece).
sentient_harm_explanation: Each dairy goat must give birth about once a year to keep producing milk, and is killed once her yield drops, after roughly five years of milking. Only about one of her kids is kept to replace her; the others are raised for meat and killed at around a year old. Per goat we count her own death plus about four kids. No goat brain has been counted, so the neuron count is estimated from goat brain size using counts from related hoofed animals.

name: Goat Cheese
notes:
Soft goat cheese (chèvre), nutrition from USDA. Built exactly like cheddar, but on the goat milk entry. FAO's goat-cheese extraction rate is a median of 17% across 21 countries (range 5–30%), so ~5.9 kg of goat milk per kg. After the whey's 4.8% share, goat cheese carries 5.6 kg of goat milk per kg. Every per-kg goat-milk impact is × 5.6.

Because the world-average milking goat gives so little milk, each goat's whole life yields only ~91 kg of cheese. The deaths of the goat and her ~4.2 kids are spread over very little food, and goat cheese is the lowest-scoring food in the dataset. Cheese from French or US commercial dairy goats would score noticeably better.

CO2 adds Poore & Nemecek's cheese processing, transport, retail and packaging, as for cheddar. Availability is FAOSTAT world goat cheese production (~461 kt a year; France ~90 kt).
land_types_note: Same land as goat milk: grazing and crop stubble in semi-arid South Asia, NE Africa and the Sahel, plus Mediterranean and western European dairy goats (France is the largest goat cheese maker).
sentient_harm_explanation: Goat cheese is made from goat milk, so it carries the same animal deaths as goat milk. It takes about 6 kg of goat milk to make 1 kg of soft goat cheese; the whey is sold too, so goat cheese is charged about 5.6 kg of milk per kg. Each dairy goat must give birth about once a year to keep producing milk and is killed once her yield drops; only about one of her kids is kept to replace her and the rest are raised for meat. Per goat we count her own death, about 4.2 kids at roughly 1.3 years old each, and a lifetime share of only about 91 kg of goat cheese, because the world-average milking goat gives little milk. No goat brain has been counted, so the neuron count is estimated from goat brain size using counts from related hoofed animals.

name: Heavy Cream
notes:

sentient_harm_explanation: Cream Cheese is made from cow's milk (about 4.6 kg of milk's value per kg of cream cheese), so it carries the same animal deaths as milk. name: Ice Cream
notes:
Regular vanilla ice cream (~11% fat), nutrition from USDA. The milk side is cow milk × 1.8 kg of milk per kg (fat takes 37% and protein 63% of a milk's value, as in the butter entry: 11/3.7 × 0.373 + 3.5/3.3 × 0.627). It carries the same cow and calf deaths as milk.

Added sugar (~0.15 kg of cane sugar per kg, confidence 1) is charged through the crop-input rows. Eggs, stabilisers and vanilla are ignored. CO2 adds 1.0 kg CO2e/kg for mixing, freezing, hardening and frozen storage (educated guess, confidence 1). US availability is USDA's October 2024 production annualised; the world figure is a confidence-1 guess.
land_types_note: Pasture and feed crops in the US, Europe and NZ (grassland and long-cleared forest), with some Brazilian soy in feed.
sentient_harm_explanation: Ice Cream is made from cow's milk (about 1.8 kg of milk's value per kg of ice cream), so it carries the same animal deaths as milk. Each dairy cow must give birth roughly every year to keep producing milk; only about one of her calves is kept to replace her, and the rest die young or are raised and killed for veal or beef. Per cow we count: her own death (about 5 years old in the US; longer worldwide), about 2.1 calves in the US or 3.5 worldwide at roughly 1.5 years old each, and a lifetime of about 17,650 kg of ice cream in the US or 7,500 kg worldwide.

name: Swiss Cheese
notes:
Swiss cheese (Emmental type), nutrition from USDA. Every per-kg impact is cow milk × 10.4 kg of milk per kg of cheese. The milk-equivalent comes from cheese's protein (26.96 g per 100 g) ÷ (milk protein 3.3 g × 75% recovered into the curd) = 10.9, × 0.952 because the whey that cheese-making throws off is sold and takes ~4.8% of the burden (the same adjustment the Cheddar entry uses: 9.2 → 8.8). That method gives 9.3 for Cheddar, matching USDA's 9.2. It carries the same animal deaths as the milk.

CO2 adds 1.38 kg CO2e/kg for cheese-making, ageing and packaging, the same Poore & Nemecek processing figure as Cheddar. The world emissions benchmark is Poore & Nemecek's all-cheese average (23.88, built on ~8.8 kg of milk per kg) scaled to this cheese's milk need: 28.3 (confidence 1). Availability is USDA's US Swiss cheese output annualised from October 2024, plus a confidence-1 world guess (~5% of world cow-milk cheese).

name: Feta
notes:
Feta, nutrition from USDA. Every per-kg impact is goat milk × 5.5 kg of milk per kg of cheese. The milk-equivalent comes from cheese's protein (14.21 g per 100 g) ÷ (milk protein 3.3 g × 75% recovered into the curd) = 5.7, × 0.952 because the whey that cheese-making throws off is sold and takes ~4.8% of the burden (the same adjustment the Cheddar entry uses: 9.2 → 8.8). That method gives 9.3 for Cheddar, matching USDA's 9.2. It carries the same animal deaths as the milk.

CO2 adds 1.38 kg CO2e/kg for cheese-making, ageing and packaging, the same Poore & Nemecek processing figure as Cheddar. There is no published emissions benchmark for feta or goat's-milk cheese (the goat milk and goat cheese entries have none either), so emissions are built only from the gas and feed rows. Traditional feta is made from sheep's milk (often mixed with goat's milk), and the dataset has no sheep entry, so this one is built on the goat milk entry (a rough stand-in; US feta is often made from cow's milk). Availability is USDA's US feta output annualised from October 2024, plus a confidence-1 world guess.
land_types_note: Mostly grazing and crop stubble in semi-arid India, Pakistan, Sudan and the Sahel; plus Mediterranean and western European dairy goats (France, Spain, Netherlands, Greece).
sentient_harm_explanation: Feta is made from goat's milk (about 5.5 kg of milk per kg of feta), so it carries the same animal deaths as the milk. Each dairy goat must give birth roughly every year to keep producing milk; the offspring not kept as replacements are killed young or raised and killed for meat. Per animal we count its own death, its offspring and a lifetime output of about 93 kg of feta worldwide.
